one_liner: Header-only C++17 fixed-capacity, single-type pool with intrusive free list; about 10x faster than MSVC malloc/free on alloc-free pairs.
what_it_does: alloc::PoolAllocator<T, N> holds N slots of max(sizeof(T), sizeof(void*)) bytes inline in the object and hands them out one at a time: allocate()/deallocate() return and take raw T* storage, create(args...)/destroy() add placement-new construction and explicit destruction, and owns(), used(), capacity() and reset() round out the API. It is not an std::allocator and not a malloc replacement; you call the pool directly for one object type with a compile-time capacity, and allocate() returns nullptr when full.
how_it_is_fast: Classic fixed-size pool (segregated free list): free slots store a next pointer inside themselves, so allocation pops the list head and deallocation pushes onto it, a few loads and stores with no size lookup, no locking and no header. Storage is a contiguous inline array, so a LIFO alloc/free loop keeps reusing one hot cache line. Against Windows UCRT malloc (a heap call per request) that is enough for about 2.7 ns vs 28 ns per pair.
when_to_use: Single-threaded code that churns one small object type (nodes, messages, particles) with a known upper bound on live objects.
Hot loops on Windows/MSVC where the CRT heap is the bottleneck and the objects never escape a single owner.
Embedded or no-heap settings where a static, compile-time-sized arena for one type is wanted.
As a teaching-sized (about 130 lines) pool to copy into a project and adapt.
when_not_to_use: Any multi-threaded use: there are no atomics or locks, and thread-safety is not documented.
Mixed sizes or types, or an unknown maximum count: capacity is the template argument N and allocate() returns nullptr when exhausted, with no growth.
Large N on the stack: slots_ is an inline array, so PoolAllocator<int, 100000> as used in the benchmark is 800 KB of stack, near the 1 MB Windows default.
Code that needs std::allocator or pmr integration, or drop-in replacement of malloc/new.
As evidence of beating mimalloc or glibc: only MSVC UCRT malloc was compared, and modern general allocators have thread-local fast paths for this pattern.

integration.dependencies: none (Google Test and Google Benchmark via vcpkg only for tests/bench)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (uses std::byte); built with MSVC 2022, CMake 3.20+ for the project files
integration.platforms: any (portable C++17; only tested on Windows 11 x64 per README)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no synchronization in the code, so not thread-safe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explicit pool object with allocate/deallocate or create/destroy for one type T; not a malloc/new replacement

gotchas: reset() is O(N), not O(1): it re-links all N slots every call, and it does not run destructors of live objects; the destructor also leaves live objects undestroyed.
deallocate() checks ownership only with assert, so in Release builds a foreign pointer or a double free silently corrupts the free list.
allocate() returns uninitialised storage cast to T*; use create() for non-trivial types. The free-list links are accessed through reinterpret_cast without std::launder.
N = 0 is not rejected and the constructor then indexes slots_[N - 1].
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over fast-alloc (NotKeira) or atul-singh-as/custom-memory-allocator only if you want the smallest single-header, single-type pool with create/destroy and owns(); for anything thread-safe or general-purpose, use a real allocator such as mimalloc or a TLSF like XenoAtom.Allocators, and for scoped bulk lifetime an arena such as cleeus/obstack.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run Google Benchmark on an Intel i5-12450H, Windows 11, MSVC 2022 x64-Release (flags not stated): 1024 LIFO int alloc+free pairs take 2,731 ns vs 29,067 ns with malloc/free (about 2.7 vs 28 ns per pair), 256 std::string create+destroy take 7,240 vs 19,826 ns, and 10,000 bulk allocations take 54,860 vs 433,902 ns; the 188M vs 23M ops/s throughput row matches the bulk-10,000 row restated as items per second (derived from page data). In the bulk test the pool side releases with reset(), which re-links all 100,000 slots each iteration, while malloc frees each pointer, so the two sides do different release work.
status_note: Active but brand-new (3 commits, 0 stars, last commit 2026-09-29); MIT-licensed and tiny, so copyable, but a learning-project pool rather than a hardened allocator.
